name: Grove Vibration Motor (v1.2)
description: 10 mm coin vibration motor (ANDA-B1020, 3 V rated, about 60 mA) on a Grove board with its own transistor driver: SIG goes through 1 kΩ to an S9013 NPN transistor (100 kΩ base pull-down), which switches the motor from VCC through a 12 Ω series resistor. SIG high = vibrate, low or unconnected = off; PWM on SIG sets the strength. Works from 3.0–5.5 V, so a 3.3 V GPIO can drive it directly. Sold as: Seeed Studio Grove - Vibration Motor v1.2 (SKU 105020003), 4-pin Grove connector SIG, NC, VCC, GND.
eli5: A tiny buzzing motor like the one in a phone: set the pin high and it shakes, set it low and it stops.

pins.name: SIG
pins.description: Control input (Grove pin 1, yellow wire): high = vibrate, low = off; PWM sets the strength. Drives the S9013 base through 1 kΩ (about 2.6 mA from a 3.3 V GPIO); a 100 kΩ pull-down keeps the motor off when unconnected.

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: Motor supply (Grove pin 3, red wire): 3.0–5.5 V. The motor current (about 50–80 mA, up to ~110 mA at start) comes from this pin, not from SIG.

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Ground (Grove pin 4, black wire), shared with the microcontroller.

buildNotes: Grove connector order (Seeed schematic J1): pin 1 SIG (yellow), pin 2 NC (white), pin 3 VCC (red), pin 4 GND (black). The board has a 2 mm Grove socket, not header pins: use a Grove-to-female-jumper cable to reach the breadboard.
Circuit (Seeed v1.2 Eagle schematic): SIG → 1 kΩ → S9013 NPN base, 100 kΩ base-to-GND pull-down; motor + to VCC, motor − through 12 Ω to the collector. High = vibrate, low or floating = off.

VCC 3.3 V or 5 V both work (Seeed spec 3.0–5.5 V). On 5 V it buzzes harder; on 3.3 V the motor draws about 50 mA, on 5 V about 80 mA, with up to about 110 mA for a moment at start-up (ANDA-B1020 datasheet).
The flyback diode footprint D1 is marked DNP (not fitted) on the v1.2 schematic. The coin motor's small inductance makes this tolerable, but avoid very fast PWM; about 1 kHz or lower is fine.
For gentler buzzing use PWM on SIG (machine.PWM at about 1 kHz with lower duty); the motor needs about 2.3 V across it to start, so very low duty may not spin it up.
Older v1.0 boards (2011) drive the motor straight from the I/O pin without a transistor; this part models v1.2 and later.

example.code:
from machine import Pin
import time

motor = Pin({SIG}, Pin.OUT, value=0)  # SIG high = vibrate
while True:
    motor.value(1)
    print('VIBRATE ON')
    time.sleep(1)
    motor.value(0)
    print('VIBRATE OFF')
    time.sleep(2)

test.title: The motor switches on, then off again
